abstractText:
The query optimizer is a core component of database servers, which represent one of the most successful products of the software industry, adopted massively both across business enterprises and in scientific projects ranging from astronomy to genomics. Despite this success and decades of work, query optimization is still far from solved. The main reasons are the complexity of the problem and the fast pace of hardware development, which makes query optimization a continuously moving target. In this project, the researchers investigate how to design COMPASS, a lightweight, yet effective, query optimizer for modern databases based on two design principles. The first principle is to capitalize on highly-parallel computing architectures in query optimization, while the second is to simplify the type and number of synopses included in the optimizer. The final goal is to build COMPASS, an open-source query optimizer that can be integrated into existing and novel database servers. Due to the extensive use of databases across many domains of modern life, optimal querying can bring benefits to the entire society.

COMPASS is an online query optimizer that uses sketch synopses exclusively in order to find optimal execution plans. Sketches are correlated synopses for cardinality estimation that use small space, can be computed efficiently in a single scan over the data, are linearly composable, and have statistically high accuracy. COMPASS uses the parallel execution engine in modern databases to  compute sketches at runtime. This is realized by decomposing query processing into two stages, performed before and after optimization. In the first execution stage, selection predicates are pushed-down and sketches are built only over the relevant tuples. Plan enumeration is performed over the join graph by incrementally composing two-way join sketches in order to estimate the cardinality of multi-way joins. The plan is executed in the second processing stage. The holistic COMPASS approach introduces novel methods in all the components of the query optimizer---cardinality estimation for selections, two-way, and multi-way joins; plan enumeration; and cost models. In addition to the algorithmic aspects, these methods involve heavy engineering practices on highly-parallel architectures. Specifically, parallel random number generation schemes go well beyond sketches due to their application to many other data processing tasks. This is also applicable to graph traversal algorithms. The generalization of sketches to multi-way join estimation has intellectual value by itself because this is a theoretical open problem. Since sketches are streaming algorithms at origin, the contributions made in this project are also directly applicable to this area.

projectOutComesReport:
This project has investigated novel query optimization techniques for relational databases, which are used extensively in daily life by businesses, research institutions, and government agencies alike. The project made contributions across the entire query optimization spectrum, from cardinaity estimation to cost models and plan enumeration.

First, we introduced three sketch-based cardinality estimators for multi-way join queries with filters. The first estimator supports arbitrary filter conditions that are evaluated during query processing using GPU accelerators. The other two estimators use machine learning models to learn the distribution of the join conditioned on the filters. The first learned estimator uses autoregressive models while the second uses sum-product networks. We integrated all these estimators in PostgreSQL, the most popular open-source database, and obtained state-of-the-art results on widely accepted benchmarks.

Second, we designed the permutation-based L1-error cost model for the identification of sub-optimal query execution plans. L1-error requires complete knowledge of true cardinalities and estimates for all the sub-plans of a query plan, which renders it applicable only to post-execution analysis. To address this issue, we developed a robust incremental classification model to predict plan sub-optimality. This model employs a transformer architecture to learn positional discrepancies between the sub-plan order vector and the optimal order, achieving high accuracy above 90% in identifying sub-optimal plans.

Third, we developed two graph-based join ordering algorithms. The Simplicity Simplified (Simpli-Squared) algorithm achieves unexpectedly good results without using any statistics or cardinality estimates. Simpli-Squared computes the optimal join order from the query graph and the size of the base tables using a lightweight query rewriting procedure. The Ensemble Spanning Tree Enumeration (ESTE) strategy enumerates multiple query plans by exploring different areas of the search space. This positions ESTE as an intermediate strategy between exhaustive and heuristic enumeration strategies. In the case of data and workload changes, ESTE can be a cheaper alternative to maintain optimizer robustness by integrating additional spanning tree algorithms rather than completely changing the optimizer to another plan enumeration algorithm.

The findings of this project are published in prestigious journals, conference proceedings and workshops, as well as in the open arXiv repository. The most important accomplishments include three publications in ACM SIGMOD, the premier data management conference in the world. Additionally, all the artifacts, including source code, datasets, workloads, and benchmarks are released in the public domain. Moreover, these materials have been used in courses taught by the PI at UC Merced.

The project provided financial support to four Ph.D. students at various stages in their academic career. Two of these students graduated and pursued careers in academia and industry, respectively.

abstractText:
Nontechnical Summary

This project supports theoretical research and education on the implementation of a special purpose quantum computer with practical devices.

Quantum computers with 50-100 qubits and decoherence times not long enough for general-purpose quantum computing can now be built in laboratories. With such devices, a quantum simulator, a special-purpose quantum computer, may be able to solve problems that cannot be solved with classical computers. A prerequisite to implementing quantum simulation is to prepare the simulator in an appropriate many-body ground state, something that could also benefit the solution of combinatorial optimization problems.  These many-body states are often unknown, highly entangled, and hard to prepare with quantum logic gates. Despite previous efforts, it remains a challenging question to prepare such many-body states with high fidelity.  The PI aims to develop a universal and implementable algorithm to efficiently and accurately generate such many-body ground states by coupling the quantum simulator to an auxiliary system that induces nonlinearity. This novel approach exploits a generic but unique property of nonlinear systems to suppress unwanted transitions between the ground state and the excited states. The objectives of this project include the development of the general framework for the algorithm, benchmarking the algorithm, and studying the effect of circuit noise. The algorithm will be tested on four models that represent problems of different interests in quantum simulation. Both numerical simulation using classical computers and hardware emulation using a superconducting cloud platform will be employed to test the algorithm. Because it exploits generic nonlinear dynamics, this algorithm can be applied to a broad range of problems.

The project not only has potential scientific impact on quantum computing and quantum simulation, but it can also open the door to a new direction that uses nonlinear physics for efficient quantum computing. The educational component of this project will broaden the participation of women and minority students and improve the diversity of the workforce in quantum technology. The PI will develop a course on advanced quantum computing, actively recruit students and postdocs from underrepresented groups, and organize activities with the women-in-STEM group and the Society of Physics Students at UC Merced. These activities will engage students at UC Merced, a Hispanic serving institute, in quantum research.


Technical Summary

This project supports theoretical research and education on the implementation of quantum simulation with noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices.

A quantum simulator is a special-purpose quantum computer that can solve classically-hard problems. Efficient preparation of a many-body system in its ground state is a prerequisite for exploring quantum dynamics and many-body correlations in quantum simulators. Understanding the feasibility and limits on state preparation also benefits the study of combinatorial optimization problems in adiabatic quantum computing. Despite previous efforts, it remains a challenging question to prepare many-body states with high fidelity due to the lack of knowledge of the energy spectrum, the rapid decrease of energy gaps with the size of the quantum simulator, and the limited decoherence times in practical devices.  The PI aims to develop a universal and implementable algorithm to efficiently and accurately generate many-body ground states by coupling a quantum simulator to an auxiliary system that induces nonlinearity. This novel approach exploits the unique dynamics in the vicinity of bifurcation points, which is a generic property in nonlinear systems, to enable self-governed adiabatic evolution with significantly suppressed diabatic transitions. The project includes three objectives: 1. developing the generic framework, operational protocol, and requirements on the quantum circuits for the algorithm, 2. benchmarking the algorithm and comparing its performance with other methods, and 3. qualitatively studying the effect of circuit noise. The algorithm will be tested on four models representing different interests in quantum simulation: the transverse-field Ising model, an exact-cover problem, a finite-sized Jaynes-Cummings lattice, and toy models with multiple energy gaps.  Both numerical simulation and hardware emulation using the IBM Q cloud platform will be employed to test the algorithm. Because it exploits generic nonlinear dynamics, this algorithm can be applied to a broad range of problems without knowledge of the energy spectrum or the construction of unphysical multipartite interactions.

The project not only has potential scientific impact on quantum computing and quantum simulation, but it can also open the door to a new direction that uses nonlinear physics for efficient quantum computing. The educational component of this project will broaden the participation of women and minority students and improve the diversity of the workforce in quantum technology. The PI will develop a course on advanced quantum computing, actively recruit students and postdocs from underrepresented groups, and organize activities with the women-STEM group and the Society of Physics Students at UC Merced. These activities will engage students at UC Merced, a Hispanic serving institute, in quantum research.

projectOutComesReport:
Main outcomes:

Preparing quantum many-body states with high fidelity and resiliency against control errors and noise is fundamental but challenging question in quantum computing.  The major goal of this EAGER project is to pave the road to develop a universal and implementable algorithm to efficiently and accurately generate many-body ground states by coupling quantum simulators to an auxiliary system (i.e., ancilla) that induces nonlinearity. We exploited the unique dynamics in the vicinity of bifurcation points, a generic property in nonlinear systems to enable self-governed adiabatic evolution with significantly suppressed diabatic transitions.  Meanwhile, we also explored various quantum control techniques, including an optimized adiabatic approach, quantum optimal control approach and quantum shortcuts to adiabaticity, to deepen our understanding of this fundamental question. We have accomplished the main objective of this project. We have developed the theory for the self-governed adiabatic evolution, have published several journal articles, and have obtained preliminary results to be published.

The journal articles we have published or submitted include:

K. Cai, P. Parajuli, G.-L. Long, C.-W. Wong, and L. Tian, “Robust Preparation of Many-body Ground States in Jaynes-Cummings Lattices”, nature partner journal Quantum Information 7, 96 (2021).

J.-F. Huang and L. Tian, “Modulation-based superradiant phase transition in the strong-coupling regime”, PRA 107, 063713 (2023).

Cheng Liu, Jin-Feng Huang, and Lin Tian, “Deterministic generation of multi-photon bundles in a quantum Rabi model”, Science China Phys. Mech. Astro. 66, 220311 (2023).

P. Parajuli, A. Govindarajan, and L. Tian, “State preparation in a Jaynes‑Cummings lattice with quantum optimal control”, Sci. Rep. 13, 19942 (2023).

K. Cai, P. Parajuli, A. Govindarajan, and L. Tian, “Quantum Shortcut to Adiabaticity for State Preparation in a Finite-Sized Jaynes-Cummings Lattice”, PRA 110, 022621 (2024).

L. Tian, A. Govindarajan, P. Parajuli, and K. Cai, “Quantum state preparation in Jaynes-Cummings lattices”, J. Phys.: Conf. Ser. 2912, 012041 (2024).

A. Govindarajan and L. Tian, “Local Counterdiabatic Driving for Jaynes-Cummings Lattices”, arXiv:2409.19186.

The manuscripts that we are preparing or the preliminary results that we obtained include:

K. Yip, S. Ashhab, and L. Tian, “Emulating Holstein Primakoff Transformation with Noisy Qubits”, in preparation.

A. Govindarajan and L. Tian, “Quantum Optimal Control for JC Lattices” (tentative title), in preparation.

A. Govindarajan, M. Mazzei, Hailin Wang, and L. Tian, “Continuous-variable cluster states in Phononic Quantum Network”, in preparation

L. Tian, “A Universal and Implementable Approach to Quantum Adiabaticity”, in revision

The educational and student training outcomes include:

Teaching. The PI developed a course on advanced quantum computing. This course was first offered in Spring 2021 to graduate students (PHYS274) and will be offered every other year and can help us expand the quantum efforts at UC Merced. We recently developed this course into an undergraduate version by creating PHYS174, which will be offered conjointly with PHYS274. This is the first course on this topic at UC Merced. This course teaches concepts of quantum computing, quantum algorithm, adiabatic quantum computing, quantum simulation, and physical systems (especially superconducting quantum devices). It aims to give students basic training on quantum computing and quantum technology as well as make students familiar with recent progresses in this field. This course is offered regularly at UC Merced.

Graduate student training.  This project can improve the diversity of the quantum taskforce by training students from diverse backgrounds. Five graduate students have worked on this project. Among these students, two have graduated (one is a minority student), the third student (female student) has passed qualify exam and is graduating in Spring 2025, and two students have passed pre-qualifying exam in August 2024. 

Undergraduate student training. The PI served as faculty advisor for 3 REU students (2 in summer 2023, 1 in summer 2024) on the topic “IBM Cloud Simulation of  the 1-D Transverse Field Ising Model”.  In 2023, a REU student from San Diego State University won the APS Helen Quinn Award for Education or Undergraduate Research Theory for his presentation “Simulating the Quantum Ising Model with Cloud Quantum Computers”. In 2024, a REU student from Univ. Washington won the APS Helen Quinn Award for Education or Undergraduate Research Theory for her presentation “IBM Cloud Simulation of the 1D Transverse Field Ising Model”.

abstractText:
Population growth and changing climates have made it difficult to ensure equitable access to food, water, and economic security across the globe, particularly for women and vulnerable communities. In southern Morocco, rural women engage in the production of argan oil that is extracted from the nuts of an indigenous tree. As both an edible and cosmetic product in high demand on the world market, argan provides a source of food and income to local communities and benefits the environment by conserving argan trees that prevent erosion and desertification. Through an interdisciplinary field school over three summers, U.S. students will conduct research with Moroccan faculty and students to investigate environmental and socioeconomic aspects of women’s argan production. This project provides professional development opportunities for 18 U.S. students in undergraduate and graduate programs in Environmental Engineering and Systems and Anthropology at UC Merced and USF. USF and UC Merced have partnered with Dar Si Hmad for Development, Education and Culture and Université Ibn Zohr in Agadir, Morocco to provide international research experience for students. The skills and experience students gain through this project will be applicable to other food and livelihood systems in the United States and throughout the world.    

The overall goal of this collaborative USF-UC Merced IRES project is to train an interdisciplinary workforce to research and design socially and environmentally sustainable and equitable systems. Specific objectives of USF-UC Merced IRES are to: (1) Provide interdisciplinary summer research opportunities between environmental engineers and scientists and anthropologists, (2) Educate students in environmental and social life cycle assessment (E-LCA and S-LCA) and thinking to better design systems, (3) Train students in household livelihood systems approaches and ethnographic and qualitative research methods, (4) Exchange research findings with host communities and partner institutions to improve the environmental sustainability and socioeconomic benefits of argan oil production as a model for other food systems, (5) Increase the amount of underrepresented minorities, women, and lower income students that participate in international research and improve the long-term global competency of the U.S. workforce, and (6) Strengthen collaboration between the United States and international institutions in Morocco.

projectOutComesReport:
Argan trees, Argania spinosa (L.), have existed for over 80 million years in North Africa. In Morocco, the argan forest area covers approximately 800,000 ha of land in a biosphere designated by UNESCO in 1998. The argan tree holds important symbolic and economic value for indigenous Amazigh communities in southern Morocco. Rural women in these communities inhabit villages near the argan forests and have been harvesting and processing argan oil for decades as part of their traditional foodways. Women collect and crack argan nuts with rocks and extract oil from the argan kernels using stone mills. The oil is used for edible and cosmetic purposes and sold to local, national, and international markets at high prices. Argan oil contributes nutrition and income to local households and provides economic development strategies for women in the region and incentives to conserve the tree. The argan industry employs some of the lowest income earning populations in rural Morocco and thus plays a key role in promoting poverty reduction. 

The overall goal of this project was to train engineers, scientists, and anthropologists to research and design socially and environmentally sustainable and equitable systems to improve argan production in Morocco. Over three years, the field school provided international research experience to 19 undergraduate and graduate students in engineering, environmental systems, and social sciences from University of South Florida and University of California Merced. Participants included 68% women and 53% of underrepresented minorities (Black/African-American and Hispanic), which contributed to increasing the diversity and long-term global competency of the U.S. workforce in science, engineering and technology. 

Students conducted 4-5 weeks of field research each summer (2022-2024) on sustainable argan production in partnership with Foundation Dar Si Hmad in Agadir, Morocco and faculty and students in sociology, engineering, geography, and English at Universite Ibn Zohr in Agadir. The main research areas included: environmental and social life cycle assessment of argan oil production; a household level study of the socioeconomic benefits and challenges of different types of argan production; mapping and geospatial analyses of the argan forest (land suitability, production potential, and potential impacts of climate change and urbanization); and evaluation and design of labor saving technologies and workplace safety considerations for argan oil production. Student participants worked on the three interdisciplinary research thrusts in life cycle assessment, geospatial analysis, and ethnographic teams. Graduate students mentored undergraduates and the social scientists and engineers helped to educate each other in their respective fields, which allowed them to share skills in a real-world professional setting.

The intensive program included training in local languages and cross-cultural skills, lectures by Moroccan professors, visits to a local argan museum and argan machinery shop, meetings with Moroccan representatives and scientists (agronomists and geographers) from national agencies for agricultural research and argan development, and discussions with members of the Argan Rights Holders Association on land tenure issues. Students received hands-on methods training in life cycle assessment, geospatial analysis, household livelihood systems approaches, qualitative research (observation, interviewing, and note-taking), and survey research (survey design, sampling, survey administration, data entry, and analysis). During the data collection phase, they worked in interdisciplinary teams to conduct 68 total household surveys in rural villages located in three main regions of the argan zone (Sidi Ifni, Essaouira, and Agadir), focus group discussions with leaders and members of 16 argan cooperatives, interviews at 22 argan retail shops in five cities, and participant observation in multiple field sites. 

The study has made several innovative contributions to current argan research, including the first environmental life cycle assessment of argan oil (forthcoming in the International Journal of Life Cycle Assessment). Students added new indicators to the social life cycle assessment of argan oil by incorporating human energy, impact of technology, and workplace pain and injuries. The comparative household survey assessed the needs and challenges of women argan producers working in households, cooperatives, and market retail shops in different areas of the Moroccan argan zone. Students presented preliminary findings to Moroccan partners and shared their experiences with the public through a website, blog, and documentary video (sustainableargan.org). Students and faculty have presented research results at seven major academic conferences in the US and Canada and a specialized international conference on the argan tree.  

The broader social impacts of this project include evidence-based recommendations to improve: (1) sustainable development practices for conserving argan trees as part of the environmental and cultural heritage of Morocco; (2) the situation of women producers in the argan industry, including cooperative structures and issues of workplace safety, labor, fair trade, and forms of social and economic empowerment; and (3) techniques in manual and mechanized oil processing; (4) best practices in business and cooperative models for argan production and commercialization. The methods developed and findings of the study are also applicable to similar small-scale industries in Morocco and other developing economies.

abstractText:
Bacterial biofilms are multicellular communities that display coordinated collective behaviors and emergent pattern formations. They present an important and outstanding challenge in daily life in view of their prevalence in health and industrial problems such as antimicrobial resistance, infection and biofouling of water pipes and ship hulls, which pose severe economic burdens. Many functions of the cell, including adhesion, migration, and multicellular organization, can be altered by changes in the physical properties of the cellular environment. The physical and molecular mechanisms by which cells sense and respond to physical stimuli are poorly understood. The aim of this proposal is to develop a synthetic hydrogel system and use it for assessing the effects of substrate mechanics on biofilm development. The results of this project will provide insight into mechanisms of biofilm growth and how to control its behavior. Furthermore, this project trains a diverse set of undergraduate and graduate students as well as provides research opportunities for high school teacher interns. Teacher-interns participate in on-going research projects in the lab as well as in laboratory and department seminars to facilitate exchange of ideas on education and research. In addition, they are developing a curriculum, based on their projects, that is applied in their own classrooms.

The overarching goal of this project is to determine how physical properties of the cellular microenvironment regulate biofilm development within Myxococcus xanthus. A major limitation in this type of study is a lack of appropriate in vitro materials to quantify the effects of systemic changes in substrate mechanics on biofilm development. This project creates new synthetic hydrogel systems, with well-defined tunable chemical and mechanical properties, and uses them to determine the direct response of cells to specific chemical and mechanical stimuli. Models of bacteria-substrate interactions are tested in unprecedented ways. The project integrates experimental and computational approaches, to build and test predictive models of bacterial biofilm development and the functional roles played by the cellular environment.

projectOutComesReport:
The central goals of the collaborative project were to study the biophysical mechanisms underlying various stages in the spreading of bacteria biofilms and colonies on soft elastic substrates with tunable properties. From the perspective of simulations and modeling, the project sought to design, test, and implement efficient and multi-scale computational models to interpret and guide experiments on  bacteria colonies and suspensions interacting with surfaces. The primary hypothesis driving the modeling effort is that interaction of bacteria with bounding surfaces combined with mechanical sensing of substrate properties, and cell-cell interactions determine the properties and dynamics of the colony. The biophysical parameters that play a crucial role in this process include the viscous properties of the fluidic medium in which bacteria swim, the shape and size of the bacteria cells, and cell-boundary and cell-substrate interactions. A suite of versatile, multi-scale and highly efficient numerical schemes were developed that allowed for independent exploration of the impact of these parameters on the dynamics of bacterial colonies. The computations fell broadly within two categories. The first category included detailed micro-scale stochastic mixed-mode simulations based on Brownian dynamics coupled with fluid hydrodynamics solvers to track the movement, growth and interaction between individual cells interacting mechanically with the ambient environment. The second included efficient, parallel, adaptive level-set based computations that solve meso-scale continuum models for the bacterial colonies; these enabled us to model the spatiotemporal evolution and organization at large scales. In parallel, high-speed and high-resolution microscopy experiments to track the evolution of a colony starting from single cells, to growing jammed clusters, and eventually to flowing swarms or stationary biofilms were developed and implemented. Broadly, the techniques developed as a part of this grant are generalizable to a wide variety of active matter including autonomous biomimetic agents, motile eukaryotic cells, and blood clots. 

Taken together, the computational methods developed, and simulations or experiments conducted as a part of this project, enabled discoveries and key insights. Among the techniques developed and discoveries that were made over the course of the grant are: 1) Developed a hybrid computational method that combines discrete agent-based cell description with continuum fluid hydrodynamics and idealized cell-substrate interactions. The simulations enabled the identification and discovery of the individual and synergistic roles played by cell morphology, direct cell interactions, and fluid mediated cell-cell and cell-substrate interactions in the onset and maintenance of structure in colonies. These results are relevant to understanding how mixing, cell motility, and phenotypical adaptation impact such active fluids and solids. 2) Developed a parallel adaptive highly efficient solver for modeling confined multi-population or multi-phenotype active fluids and colonies. Discovered via phase-plot explorations that hydrodynamics dominates the dissolution mechanism. In silico explorations reproduced experimental patterns for colonies including active dissolution in mixed partially mobile systems. The results suggest that bacterial cells may use fluidization to transition locally from a fixed biofilm state to a motile state.  3) Discovered that bacterial colony and biofilm growth rates can increase with stiffness for synthetic hydrogel and polymeric substrates such as polyacrylamide gels unlike what is found on traditional agar substrates. Evidence from experiments as a part of this collaborative project strongly supports the hypothesis that osmotic pressure combined with substrate poroelasticity determines biofilm growth rates. Specifically, the discovery that biofilm stresses are correlated over length-scales larger than bacterial lengths, and that their strength increases with substrate stiffness has implications in mechanical crosstalk between adjacently located colonies. This discovery motivated broader studies using minimal models on substrate elasticity modulated mechanical interactions between cells. 4) Developed and implemented a new computational mean-field continuum method that allows us to prescribe and impose constraints on the maximum bacterial concentration at desired locations.  This is important to accurately capture density-dependent transitions between bacterial phenotypes such as the swarming to biofilm transition. 5) Developed theories for collective interactions between flexible tethered or pinned active filaments. Discovered that densely arrayed active filaments pinned at an interface and immersed in viscous fluid can undergo collective instabilities that result in either metachronal waves and wave-trains or kinetically arrested periodic clusters with quantifiable size and spacing. This observation is relevant to pattern formation in arrays of flexible growing bacterial cells at boundaries and to a broader class of active biopolymers.

The research pursued with the grant further provided training opportunities to four graduate students, and six undergraduates at UC Merced, a public institution with a high number of first-generation students. The research methods developed and results obtained were also incorporated in STEM outreach activities in local high schools in Merced County over the course of the award.

abstractText:
Atomic mixtures are ubiquitous in our daily life. For example, air is a mixture of nitrogen, oxygen, and other ingredients. Cooling down the air leads to liquefaction, showing a typical example of structural transitions in multi-species mixtures. The microscopic world governed by quantum physics contains mixtures of quantum particles that exhibit many exotic phenomena awaiting our exploration. There are two types of atoms in the universe, bosons and fermions. They differ by their peer-interactions: bosons tends to congregate in the quantum regime while fermions stay away from each other. Questions about the physics of a quantum mixture of both bosons and fermions have fascinated scientists for decades. Helium atoms have offered a platform for exploring quantum mixtures, however, the systems are complicated by the complex atomic interactions and challenging experiments. Nevertheless, recent advances in cooling, trapping, and manipulating atoms have successfully produced boson-fermion quantum mixtures and renewed research interest in such systems. The proposed research will investigate the structures, thermodynamics, and dynamics of the novel atomic boson-fermion mixtures. Explicitly, the research will deliver (1) a full theory of the of quantum boson-fermion mixtures, allowing a detailed analysis of the system in and out of equilibrium, (2) a description of how bosons and fermions push each other to form a homogeneous mixture like air or a separation like oil in water, and (3) an exploration and prediction of the dynamics of quantum boson-fermion mixtures driven across the different structures. Moreover, while the quantum mixtures realized by different experimental research groups are confined in different geometries, the proposed research will extract the universal behavior and elucidate the underlying mechanism. The results will reveal the novel structures and dynamics of quantum boson-fermion mixtures and advance our understanding of the many-body physics behind composite quantum systems. 

The rapid developments of trapping and manipulating multi-species atomic mixtures have made the investigation of boson-fermion mixtures an important and urgent task, and the research will deliver a timely description of the structures and dynamics of the mixtures. The phase diagrams of atomic mixtures in uniform or harmonic potentials from the framework developed in the research based on quantum field theories will explain the current and future experimental data and guide the investigations of critical phenomena in multi-species quantum systems. The simulations and analysis of the spatial structures of the mixtures will demonstrate the extraction of critical exponents from a phase-separated structure in equilibrium, and the analysis of the quantum dynamics will reveal the influence of the fermions on the vortex formation in the bosonic superfluid. The breakdown of the scaling behavior in boson-fermion mixtures will reflect the first-order structural transition, and a comparison with the conventional analyses across a second-order phase transition will reveal the size of the critical regime. The research will establish collaborations with experimental groups to characterize the structures, thermodynamics, and dynamics of atomic boson-fermion mixtures across structural transitions in different trap geometries. The theoretical framework, simulations, and results will guide and explain experiments of atomic mixtures. To promote the research and advocate public learning, the PI will present public lectures to the local communities that have high populations of under-represented minorities and will recruit minority and women students to participate in the research and increase diversity.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
Atomic mixtures are ubiquitous. For example, air is a mixture of nitrogen and oxygen and exhibits complex behavior as temperature or pressure changes. Recent progress in cooling and controlling atoms in laboratories makes it an important task to investigate ultracold atomic mixtures in the quantum regime, and this is the goal of the project. The research began with a derivation of a general theoretical framework capable of describing the structures and thermodynamics of atomic mixtures, followed by a development of numerical simulation tools capable of capturing the complex behavior at low temperatures. When the framework is applied to binary mixtures of atoms with opposite statistical behavior, various mixed or separating structures were discovered as a result of a competition between kinetic and interaction energies. The interface separating different species reveals an interesting quantity known as the healing length as the species on both sides are forbidden to enter the opposite side and result in inhomogeneity. The phase diagrams of selected atomic mixtures from the research are shown in Figure 1, which shed light on future experimental investigations. Next, atomic mixtures of two superfluids of different nature are analyzed. Through a unified description developed in the research, different phenomena previously studied in superconductors and magnetic systems can be demonstrated by ultracold atoms acting as a versatile quantum simulator. Selected profiles of atomic superfluids from the research are shown in Figure 2, further showcasing the rich structures of atomix mixtures.

By generalizing the theory to exotic geometries, such as the spherical bubble trap for atoms realized in the International Space Station, fundamental properties of atomic superfluids are shown in the research to be smoothly tunable by varying the size of the bubble trap. Moreover, the theoretical framework have been adapted to describe energy currents in quantum systems and electric currents in circuits, as illustrated in Figure 3. The generalization of the research uncovered exotic phenomena, such as local heat flow from cold to hot due to geometric effect and variation of electric current due to remnants of a symmetry. The results thus showcase the physics behind the interplay among strongly interacting quantum systems, atomic physics, computational physics, geometry, and topology.

During the support of the award, two PhD students completed their degrees and four undergraudates submitted their senior honor theses based on the research under the supervision of the PI. Among those students, two are women and three are Hispanic, which demonstrates the effort to increase diversity in physics. The research results have been documented in 13 publications in scientific journals and several presentations in professional conferences and seminars. The manuscripts of all publications have been uploaded to the arXiv online depository for free public access. The physics curriculum at University of California, Merced, which is a Hispanic Serving Institute, has been renovated to integrate quantum physics and technology (QST) into undergraduate and graduate courses to cultivate the workforce for the emerging industry and education of QST with the help of the award. The PI also broadcasted the research and QST to local communities in the California Central Valley with a high population of under-represented minorities via events at UC Merced and local schools. Moreover, the PI offered assistance to research groups from China, Poland, and Egypt that requested help to establish research programs in atomic physics based on the project.

abstractText:
The research in this project will lead to the development of an efficient computational platform that will provide valuable insight into this physical problem of light scattering. The overarching goal is to provide a toolbox that can be used by several communities to accurately compute the electromagnetic field, complementing experimental measurements. The research will advance knowledge in several fields by filling a gap in the theory and mathematical modeling of electromagnetic fields in exotic structures. The project is designed to include an interdisciplinary (computer science, physics, mathematics), team-based approach with graduate training. The team will focus on creating applied math research results that directly impact current and future experiments. The project includes activities to organize mini-symposia at conferences to foster discussions with other researchers. 
 
The goal of this project is to develop a state-of-the-art computational and mathematical platform that accurately and efficiently capture the multiscale behaviors of the electromagnetic field in plasmonic structures. Plasmonic structures are commonly made of metals and dielectrics, and exhibit at optical frequencies surface electromagnetic waves at the metal-dielectric interfaces, called surface plasmons. Over the past decades there has been a great interest to guide and confine surface plasmons in nanophotonic devices, with applications to antennas, cloaking, and others. Surface plasmons are sub-wavelength, hyper-singular near corners, and consequently highly sensitive to the geometry. Commercial software commonly used by scientists and engineers is based on the finite element method, and poorly approximates the electromagnetic near-field in these exotic structures. There is a need for an adapted mathematical framework to capture the multiple scales, and for numerical approaches for computing the electromagnetic field in plasmonic structures to avoid inaccurate predictions. This project will develop a finite element based approach to address this problem that involves specific treatments near the interface the accurately capture the surface plasmons, and a functional framework to extract the highly oscillatory behaviors of the electromagnetic near-field. Specific work includes: (1) solve plasmonic problems for any 2D geometries in a classical framework, (2) solve plasmonic problems for any 2D geometries when hyper-singular behaviors appear, and (3) extend the framework to 3D plasmonic problems and other plasmonic models. Results from this project will lead to insights into the underlying physics, develop accurate methods, and apply them to realistic problems.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
For this project, the PI (Carvalho) and graduate student (Latham) developed competitive methods to efficiently and accurately approximate electromagnetic near-fields in plasmonic structures. Plasmonic structures are commonly made of metals (silver, gold), and dielectrics (air, glass, etc.). At optical frequencies the metal's optical response can be unusual, leading to the appearance of surface electromagnetic waves at the metal-dielectric interfaces, called surface plasmons. Surface plasmons are sub-wavelength, and highly sensitive to the geometry. Therefore there is a need for multiscale models and simulation methods to avoid inaccurate predictions. This project explored how to characterize plasmonic resonances, how to capture them numerically, for various configurations (in geometry and in material).  These new methods have been successfully implemented for both for two-dimensional and three-dimensional problems, using finite elements-based methods, Trefftz methods, Plane Wave Discontinuous Galerkin methods, and analytic computations. Dissemination of the project findings have been done through 4 publications, 12 talks (by the PI and involved graduate student), and 4 software codes. The publications and software developed for this project are all publicly available on websites and GitHub to ensure access and to allow for reproducibility of results. In addition to the novel research developed in this project, the key broader impact is the training of graduate student in research. One graduate student gained valuable experience in research engaging in this project by conducting original research, publishing papers, giving talks at international conferences, and co-organizing mini-symposia. Graduate student involved in the project has advanced to candidacy. Moreover, undergraduate students have been involved as part of this project via a project-based class on mathematical modeling.

abstractText:
For many problems in science and engineering experimental data and observations do not provide a complete picture of a system's behavior and computer simulations have become an indispensable tool for studying its evolution. However, the complexity and scale of many application problems make even computer modeling a challenging task. This is particularly true when a system undergoing complex dynamics is modeled using time dependent partial differential equations. In fact, special mathematical techniques known as time integrators must be developed to ensure that the evolution of the system is reproduced on a computer with a reasonable fidelity and in a reasonable time. It is also important that such time integration algorithms have the ability to take advantage of the parallel computational capabilities offered by both supercomputers and workstations. This project will develop new time integration methods that exploit parallelism and novel mathematical ideas in order to achieve higher accuracy and better efficiency when simulating complex systems that evolve over a wide range of temporal and spatial scales. General methods applicable to problems across science and engineering will be developed as well as special schemes particularly optimized for certain applications.  The project will explore the advantages of the new numerical approaches in the context of real-world problems such as computer design of efficient engines and weather prediction. This project will also contribute to educating and mentoring undergraduate and graduate students.

Employing parallelism effectively in the spatial discretization of partial differential equations has proven to be revolutionary in computational science.  Recent developments in time integration provide an opportunity to extend these gains to the time domain. This project will combine ideas from exponential and polynomial interpolation-based temporal integration to construct new parallel time integrators. Both parallelization across the method (i.e. over each time iteration) and parallelization across time steps (i.e.  simultaneous computation of the solution over multiple time intervals) will be explored. New approaches for fine-tuning the parameters to optimize performance of the new methods will also be investigated.  The behavior of the new methods will be studied in context of real application problems such as modeling reactive flows involved in combustion.  An additional objective of this work is to provide a guide for determining which of the new techniques are best suited for problems with a given structure.

projectOutComesReport:
Understanding the dynamics of a complex system is an integral part of many scientific and engineering problems. Since experimental data and observations can be limited in providing a full picture of the system's behavior, computer simulations play an indispensable role in research. Numerical modeling is particularly important for understanding the behavior of complex systems evolving over a wide spectrum of temporal scales, such as, for instance the chemical and hydrodynamic processes constituting combustion. Simulating dynamics of these so-called stiff large scale systems requires very efficient algorithms that are particularly suited for high performance computing platforms.  This project focused on development of numerical methods that enable efficient simulations of complex large-scale stiff dynamical systems.  In particular, several novel parallel time integrators have been constructed, analyzed, implemented and tested in the course of this work.  Ideas of exponential integration and parallel-in-time methods have been combined to produce algorithms that significantly extend capabilities of current state-of-the-art temporal integrators.  In particular, we have introduced a new exponential Parareal method that provides significant parallel speedup on both hyperbolic and dispersive equations. We have also proposed a new class of implicit-exponential methods that possess the advantages of preconditioned implicit and exponential algorithms.  In addition to theoretical advances in development and analysis of new time integration methods applicable to a wide range of stiff problems, we have constructed, implemented and tested practical algorithms for computational combustion and flagellar locomotion in low Reynolds number flows.  We were able to show that using exponential and linearly implicit methods for simulating beating flagella in a fluid with low Reynolds number, provides an order-of-magnitude  efficiency gains compared to commonly used explicit integrators. We have made advances in computational combustion in two main directions.  First, we were able to develop exponential-type variable time step integrators for chemical kinetics part of combustion models.  Specifically, we have demonstrated the promise of the new exponential algorithms to deliver computational savings when applied to simulating chemistry of combustive processes that involves large number of chemical species.  Additionally, we were able to show that such methods are also promising when hydrodynamic forces are accounted for and evolved with an exponential integrator.  In fact, the numerical approach we proposed to simulate such phenomena as flame front propagation eliminates the necessity for splitting in a time integrator, and thus allows to improve accuracy and efficiency of combustion simulations.  These initial studies not only introduced new numerical approaches for computational combustion but also highlighted promising new directions of research. To summarize, the project yielded both, new numerical methods and approaches for a wide range of large-scale stiff systems of differential equations as well as concrete algorithms for important problems in combustion and low Reynolds number locomotion.

abstractText:
Scientific computing plays a central role in knowledge discovery and scientific advancement. This award will result in the acquisition of a shared high-performance computing (HPC) cluster named Pinnacles at the University of California, Merced (UCM). Building on an increasing strength in scientific computing at UCM, the nation’s first new research-intensive university of the 21st century, this project will deploy a new state-of-the-art HPC to enable exciting cutting-edge science and facilitate advanced research training that will promote the progress of science. UCM, an Hispanic Serving Institution, is also uniquely positioned to leverage the new HPC to provide access and training opportunities for students from underrepresented groups.

Pinnacles will serve as a centerpiece for high-impact work in three scientific research pillars: (1) modeling and simulation of complex systems; (2) data enabled science; and (3) numerical optimization. This shared HPC cluster will be used by researchers to advance a broad array of conventional disciplines. Indeed, senior personnel involved in the project span all three of UCM’s academic schools, with work ranging from quantum chemistry to cognitive science. With a central focus on HPC and serving as a collaboration incubator, the Pinnacles cluster will facilitate knowledge discovery by supporting researchers working in their individual research areas and enhancing interdisciplinary collaborations to strengthen advancements at the boundaries of traditional disciplines. In addition to exciting broad scientific opportunities, Pinnacles will support early career researchers and advance learning and research experience opportunities for a diverse and underserved student population.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
The Pinnacles project involved the acquisition and deployment of a shared high-performance computing (HPC) cluster named Pinnacles. The Pinnacles HPC cluster serves as a centerpiece for UC Merced research computing and a catalyst for community building among computational scientists. The Pinnacles cluster supports three core scientific research pillars: (1) modeling and simulation of complex systems; (2) data enabled science; and (3) numerical methods and model development. Pinnacles actively supports faculty-led research groups across the full spectrum of science and engineering fields at UC Merced.

Due to supply chain delays resulting from the global Covid-19 pandemic, hardware procurement was significantly impacted. Indeed, delivery and deployment of Pinnacles occured roughly 18 months later than initially planned. As a result, scientific outcomes facilitated by this project are delayed. Nevertheless, the Pinnacles cluster has been running well since and new scientific advancements are in process.

Pinnacles has served more than 800 faculty, postdoctoral, and undergraduate and graduate student users spanning several UC Merced departments. Each month Pinnacles is providing more than 2,000,000 CPU hours of computing, serving as a major provider of research support for the UC Merced community and advancing scientific exploration and discovery.

Students and post-doctorals are becoming experts at high-performance computing because of their ready access to Pinnacles. Additionally, the cluster serves as a centerpiece for developing a research computing community, which expands networking and peer learning opportunities. Pinnacles serves as a conduit for scientific exchange through periodic meetings to discuss state-of-the-art developments in HPC, interdisciplinary scientific computing seminars, and exploration of opportunities for multi-disciplinary collaborations as well as facilitating collaborations.

This award provided new capabilities that facilitate new methods and applications for the full user community. The addition of the Pinnacles cluster has enhanced UC Merced's strength in research computing. The cluster also supports a sense of community among research computing scholars on our campus, which provides opportunities for developing new collaborative and interdisciplinary resaerch directions.

abstractText:
Environmental engineering and science is a highly diverse field that uses knowledge of physics, chemistry, and biology to help protect human and ecological health. Many environmental engineers and scientists are doing research on COVID-19 to better understand of how to control the spread of the disease, as well as providing safe food and drinking water. The goal of this project is to hold a series of virtual meetings over six weeks bringing together researchers to discuss their work on COVID-19 in an integrated manner. They will also explore how inequities influence the outcomes and impact of their work. Benefits to society resulting from this work result from open source learning materials that show how different environments link to each other during the pandemic, and how to address inequities in society to come up with better solutions for sustainable communities. This meeting will feature a diverse representation of environmental engineering and science researchers.  To maximize impact, the meeting will be open to anyone in the world, and all recordings will be shared on websites and over social media.

The goal of this project is to host a series of meetings bringing together researchers from environmental engineering and science and related fields to share knowledge and discuss interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary linkages as they relate to COVID-19 and the need for developing more healthy, just, and equitable societies.  The themes for the proposed sessions will align COVID-19 and the Grand Challenges for Environmental Engineering in the 21st Century as outlined in the National Academies of Sciences Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) study which include: (1) sustainably supplying food, energy, and water, (2) creating efficient, healthy, and resilient cities, (3) designing a future without pollution and waste, (4) climate change mitigation and adaptation, and (5) fostering informed decisions and actions. The meeting presents a new model of participation in a combined asynchronous and synchronous multimedia online learning environment. Presenters will be selected to reflect the diversity of the Nation, with particular effort made to recruit presenters who are currently underrepresented in STEM. Early career post-doctoral researchers and assistant professors will be presenters and session chairs to foster career development. Participants will be encouraged to register for the certificate portion of the meeting which requires the successful completion of six quizzes related to each session. A manuscript based on the meeting will be submitted to the journal of Environmental Engineering and Science to share best practices for virtual format for meetings and the convergence of environmental engineering and science through COVID-19.

projectOutComesReport:
This collaborative project between the University of South Florida and the University of California Merced, ?Converging COVID-19, environment, health, and equity,? hosted a meeting that brought together researchers from environmental engineering and science, and related fields to share knowledge, and discuss linkages and similarities from domains of air, water, food, and the built environment as they relate to COVID-19 responses, and contexts of inequity within communities. Six 1.5 hour online sessions were held over six weeks in Fall 2020 along six themes of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine?s environmental engineering grand challenges for the 21st Century. An additional ?Youth Moving Forward? session was held in Spring 2021. The meeting included a new model of online conferences that was divided over six weeks instead of consecutive days for greater inclusivity of working parents. All sessions were recorded and included close captioning and sign language interpretation. We ensured conference presenters and moderators reflected the diversity of the U.S. population and included more junior researchers for their professional development.  

The conference had 30 faculty (majority Civil and Environmental Engineering and Environmental Sciences but some public health and humanities) at various stages in their career (Assistant, Associate, and Full) present five-minute talks along with one faculty and/or distinguished moderator for the hour-long discussion and question and answer session. There were 625 participants registered by the end of the conference. The number of unique viewers for sessions 1-6 were 190, 189, 138, 137, 156, and 130 respectively.  These viewers attended the conference from a total of 21 different countries (The Bahamas, Bangladesh, Barbados, Brazil, Canada, China, Costa Rica, Denmark, Germany, India, Jamaica, Malaysia, Mexico, Namibia, Nigeria, Singapore, Sweden, Trinidad and Tobago, Turkey, the United Kingdom, and the United States). Based on conference participant feedback, we added a Youth Moving Forward session for greater inclusion of youth. The youth session had 84 registrants and 44 attendees. Thirty-two certificates were awarded to conference participants who watched all six sessions and passed all session quizzes with greater than 80% (mostly undergraduate and graduate students and some industry professionals as well as post docs and faculty). All six sessions are available on YouTube for viewing later as well as shorter, five-minute videos for most of the speakers.

The conference provided opportunities for research. At UC Merced, an undergraduate environmental engineering student (woman) was supported for over a year and a half. The project also provided summer research fellowships to two other undergraduate environmental engineers (one woman of color and one Hispanic male). The undergraduate supported for 1.5 years took leadership for the conference quizzes and certificates and manuscript and lead the Youth Moving Forward Session. The project also supported construction of a Corsi-Rosenthal air filter that was placed at a local elementary school to reduce the spread of COVID-19 and improve indoor air quality. Outside of students directly supported on the grant and involved in conference organization, 32 students, post-docs, or faculty watched all six session and completed all six quizzes with over 80% average to receive a conference certificate. So far the project has resulted in one peer reviewed publication and two pre-prints. Results were also disseminated through two presentations to environmental engineering and science professional societies in summer 2021.

abstractText:
Mobile crowdsensing leverages mobile devices (e.g., smartphones and wearables) to collect sensing data from users and measure spatiotemporal phenomena (e.g., air quality and traffic speed). Yet, existing crowdsensing solutions are mainly built on a cloud-centric approach that raises significant security and privacy challenges. For example, accurate and real-time situational awareness of flooding and wildfires is important for incident commanders and residents to fight these natural hazards, and mobile crowdsensing can provide large-scale monitoring of hazards by pictures and/or input provided by mobile users. Although most users are willing to help, they may hesitate to participate in such a crowdsensing task due to privacy concerns, as their private information including GPS locations may be leaked during the transmissions to a cloud server or from the storage on the server. This project investigates a hardware and software architecture for aggregation-free and privacy-aware mobile crowdsensing by integrating software and hardware design, edge computing, distributed spatiotemporal optimization, and machine-learning-based privacy protection. Without aggregating raw sensor data to a central server, this project passes latent representations of user data among edge servers until they recover the data of all areas by spatiotemporal interpolation. The educational components of this project include local-outreach programs (e.g., the University Minority Mentor Program at the University of Florida and the research week fair at the University of California, Merced) and summer internships to enhance research opportunities for underrepresented populations, including minority and female students. 

This project investigates a novel software and hardware architecture that integrates spatiotemporal prediction and distributed optimization into edge computing for aggregation-free and privacy-aware mobile crowdsensing. This project designs a machine-learning pipeline that predicts sensing measurements with partially-available crowdsensed data, at the same time providing privacy-awareness without aggregating sensor data to a central server. An edge computing platform is developed to efficiently manage the above machine-learning pipeline and automatically scale up the computing resources of multiple edge servers. Two important applications, natural hazard (flood) and public health (body temperature) monitoring, will be implemented to evaluate system effectiveness and demonstrate societal impact.

projectOutComesReport:
Seven papers and one doctoral dissertation at UC Merced have been published. These papers cover three aspects, including crowdsensing-based driving anomaly detection, mobile computing, and efficient data transmissions. We have developed an Edge computing solution to implement a machine learning pipeline for driving anomaly detection based on the crowdsensed trajectories data of users. Smartphone-based driving maneuver anomaly detection has been widely studied for road safety. However, current works are mainly focused on personalized models that are trained by individual user’s data independently, ignoring the driving maneuver similarity of multiple drivers caused by road network or traffic conditions. This work processes the GPS data crowdsensed from multiple vehicles to detect driving maneuver anomaly using an auto-encoder machine learning pipeline. In addition, we collaborated with the PIs of this project, Prof. Christophe Bobda from University of Florida and Prof. Yanjie Fu from Arizona State University, on implementing the driving anomaly detection solution on a software and hardware co-design platform.

 

The research results from this project improve our understand on machine learning algorithms for processing crowdsensed data, mobile computing and efficient data transmissions. First, crowdsensed data can be processed by a machine learning pipeline to detect anomaly driving behavior detection. Data provided by most of the participants can be used to learn normal driving behaviors and the learned knowledge can be used to detect anomaly behaviors. An anomaly detection algorithm has been developed. Second, new machine learning algorithms have been developed to process the Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) sensor readings for human activity recognition. The results can be used for crowdsensing applications. Third, new rateless-coding based communication protocols have been designed and tested to provide efficient, reliable data transmissions between a pair of communication modules.

 

Our research demonstrates that smartwatches and smartphones can be used as sensors to track users' arms and identify users' daily activities, and these detection results can be collected by crowdsensing from end users in a private-preserving way. The long-term human activity monitoring results can be used by doctors to provide personalized treatment and preventive intervention. This project has supported a female PhD student at UC Merced. She has worked on the design and development of our Edge computing solution for driving anomaly detection based on the trajectories data of users. This PhD student graduated in May 2023. Two undergraduate students and one Master student have worked on the topics of this project, although they were not financially supported by this project. In addition, our team has given a talk in one of the virtual sessions for the Summer 2020 as part of our Bobcat Summer STEM Academy at UC Merced. In that talk, we introduce our research to K-12 students & teachers to enhance public understanding and increase interest in STEM from K-12 students & teachers.

abstractText:
Room-temperature ionic liquid (RTIL) lubricants derived from bio-based feedstock are environmentally benign and can offer lubrication performance superior to that of petroleum-based lubricants. However, the broad application of RTILs has been limited by the lack of a fundamental understanding of their lubrication mechanisms. Importantly, the ability of RTILs to provide adequate lubrication is determined by the preferential adsorption of RTILs on the surfaces of machine components, which in turn is affected by the interplay between surface roughness and RTIL size and structure. It is expected that, by changing the molecular structure of RTILs, the desired adsorption layer can be engineered on a given surface. This Grant Opportunities for Academic Liaison with Industry (GOALI) award will support the modeling and experimental research needed to achieve this goal. The project brings together PIs from academia with experience in tribology and tribocorrosion, biofuel and biochemical synthesis, molecular-scale simulation, and materials characterization with an industrial partner who will evaluate the RTILs in machine components and develop commercialization plans. Together, the team will achieve a new understanding of the lubrication mechanisms of RTILs that will enable design and manufacturing of bio-based lubricants with superior performance that are viable alternatives to petroleum-based products. The new RTILs will benefit industry, increasing national competitiveness, as well as society by enabling a cleaner, healthier environment. In parallel, this project will provide interdisciplinary education, research, and training opportunities for the next generation of engineers and scientists in both academic and industrial settings. 

The goal of this integrated experimental and computational project is to understand the mechanisms of RTIL lubrication for sliding surfaces with variable roughness and topography to enable design of sustainable lubricants from bio-based feedstock. The RTILs will be evaluated in terms of both their performance as lubricants and their biodegradability. Through this fundamental study, the following key scientific questions will be answered: (1) How do RTILs adsorb (form lubricating layers) on surfaces of varying roughness? (2) What tribological (friction and wear) and tribocorrosive (synergistic wear-corrosion) mechanisms are exhibited by RTIL-lubricated surfaces of varying roughness? (3) How do changes in surface topography influence RTIL lubrication mechanisms? (4) What is the role of molecular structure in the biodegradability of RTILs? Answering these questions will provide the foundational knowledge needed to overcome the current barriers to adopting RTILs as lubricants in industrial settings. This research will contribute to: (a) an in-depth understanding of the interplay between electrochemical and mechanical processes that affect material and lubricant degradation; (b) design criteria for RTIL-lubricated systems with improved tribocorrosion resistance; and (c) environmentally benign RTILs that can ultimately replace existing petroleum-based lubricants.

projectOutComesReport:
Room-temperature ionic liquid lubricants derived from bio-based feedstock are environmentally benign and can offer lubrication performance superior to that of petroleum-based lubricants. However, the broad application of these materials has been limited by a lack of fundamental understanding of their lubrication mechanisms. Therefore, the goal of this project was to develop a fundamental understanding of the mechanisms underlying the properties and performance of phosphonium ionic liquid as lubricants. The research was carried out by complementary experiments and classical molecular dynamics simulations, with input from an industrial collaborator to ensure application relevance of the results. Some of the key outcomes of the simulation aspects of the work were: (i) development of simulation protocols to predict multiple lubricant-relevant material properties of ionic liquids; (ii) observation that even small changes in the anion can significantly affect the material properties of phosphonium-based ionic liquids as well as their interactions with solid surfaces; and (iii) identification of correlations between ion structure, wettability on surfaces, and tribological performance. The experimentally corroborated simulation methods can guide the selection of anion-cation pairs for optimized tribological performance. This is particularly important given the millions of possible anion-cation combinations and the subtle relationships between chemistry, structure, and properties. The impact of this study may go beyond just lubricants, since ionic liquids are being considered for use in applications ranging from solvents to catalysis. The properties characterized in this study, such as density, viscosity, thermal conductivity, and corrosivity, are relevant to many such applications. Therefore, the structure-property-function relationships developed in this project will be broadly useful. Finally, both graduate and undergraduate students, some of whom are from underrepresented groups, received interdisciplinary training through the project. Results were disseminated to the scientific community through publications and presentations at professional conferences, as well as integrated into undergraduate-level courses on tribology.

abstractText:
People often face situations in which they must wait to learn important news.  It may be the results of a medical test, the outcome of a job interview, or the performance of financial investments. These periods can be unpleasant and stressful for many people, and a variety of (often ineffective) coping strategies may be adopted in an effort to minimize the discomfort during these uncertain waiting periods.  Past research on uncertain waiting periods has primarily focused on describing the phenomenon – identifying the emotions people feel and the coping strategies they use during these periods. What is still unknown are the reasons people choose specific coping strategies and which strategies are effective under various conditions.  Although earlier work has established that high levels of worry are the primary reason people feel distress while awaiting uncertain news, little research has tackled the questions of where this worry comes from or why people experience it so intensely during waiting periods. This project aims to answer these unanswered questions. The central premise of the research is that people experience worry during some periods of uncertainty because worry serves a purpose: It motivates people to prevent bad things from happening. However, worry can only serve this useful function when people have some control over their outcome. During uncertain waiting periods – such as that following a medical test but before learning the results – worry cannot do its job because people have no control over the outcome at that point. Eight laboratory-based experiments and one field study investigate how people cope with worry when they find themselves trapped in such stressful waiting periods.  By better understanding how people cope with the uncertainty of such situations, interventions may be developed to help reduce the discomfort and redirect energy in more productive and healthy directions.

This project develops a broad theoretical framework for understanding emotions and coping. The emotion-motivation-obstruction (EMO) model brings together two related but largely disconnected areas of study: the action readiness theory of emotions and research on situation-specific coping processes. It is proposed that when circumstances prevent people from engaging in the action tendency associated with an emotion (preventing a bad outcome in the case of worry), they will select coping strategies that aim to down-regulate the emotion or to redirect the action tendency.  By testing the EMO model in the context of worry and waiting, this research provides an instructive initial test of the framework in a domain with strong theoretical background. The project investigates how threatening uncertainty prompts worry, and in turn, its action tendency of prevention motivation and ultimately preventive behavior.  The project also focuses on situations in which preventive behavior is not feasible (due to a lack of control) and tests whether coping efforts directed toward down-regulating worry or redirecting prevention motivation reduce people’s experience of worry and the urge to carry out its action tendency.  A longer-term aim is to understand the consequences of these dynamics for health and well-being.  A multi-method experimental approach addresses these goals, using self-report, behavioral observation, and assessments of related physiological responses.  The findings of this research can serve as the basis for interventions to reduce worry and other negative emotional experiences, and to steer people toward coping strategies that are likely to be most effective for mitigating the health and well-being consequences of these experiences.

projectOutComesReport:
Throughout life, people are often faced with situations in which they must wait to learn important news—for example, about their health, professional prospects, or financial ventures. These periods are unpleasant and stressful for many people, and people adopt a variety of (often ineffective) coping strategies in an effort to minimize their discomfort during these uncertain waiting periods. The central premise of our research is that people experience worry during some periods of uncertainty because worry serves a purpose: It motivates people to prevent bad things from happening. However, worry can only serve this useful function when people have some control over their outcome. During uncertain waiting periods—like after people take an exam but before they learn their grade—worry cannot do its job because people have no control over the outcome at that point. In eight lab-based experiments and one field study, we investigated how people cope with worry when they find themselves trapped in a stressful waiting period, wracked with uncertainty and lacking control over their future.

Our project has produced outcomes in three primary categories: training, data collection, and theoretical dissemination. Regarding training, many dozens of undergraduate research assistants at both research sites have had the valuable experience of conducting tightly-designed experiments and collecting physiological data. Many of those students have gone on to graduate school (examples include students admitted to doctoral programs at the University of Michigan, University of Utah, University of Southern California, and multiple University of California and State University of California campuses), and others have leveraged their experience to attend Master’s programs or to find jobs in related fields. We have also trained 10 doctoral students in these methods.

Second, we have collected a large repository of data that we will continue to clean, analyze, and publish in the coming years. We ran over 2500 participants through our lab protocols and 200 law graduates through our field protocol. Those data include self-reports and physiological data, which have been slow to clean and prepare for analyses. Once completed, we will have a large reserve of data for publications within our labs and with collaborators, and we will post the deidentified data on the Open Science Framework for use by others in the field.

Finally, though we have not yet published or presented data from our grant-funded studies, we have been busy disseminating the theoretical concepts at their heart. We published a chapter in the second edition of the Handbook of Personal Uncertainty (Sweeny & Howell, 2025), wrote a forthcoming “Features” article for the International Society for the Study of Existential Psychology, and presented at the Existential Psychology and Health Psychology preconferences at the Society for Personality and Social Psychology (SPSP) conference as well as at the primary SPSP conference. 

We are eager to continue to dig into our large repository of data to test how people cope with worry while waiting, what their physiology reveals about those coping strategies, and how we can create effective interventions to improve waiting experiences.
